<explanation>
Based on the provided file tree and README, this project is clearly an implementation of the WebSocket protocol in Go – in other words, it’s a core WebSocket library (Gorilla WebSocket) that includes several examples to demonstrate its usage (e.g., chat, echo, command, filewatch, and autobahn for protocol compliance testing). Here’s how you can guide the design of an accurate system diagram for this project:

1. Identify the Project Type and Purpose:
   • The project is a middleware/library providing a stable and complete implementation of RFC 6455 (the WebSocket protocol) in Go.
   • The various examples (under “examples/” such as chat, echo, command, filewatch, and autobahn) are client/server/sample applications built on top of the core library. They also serve as usage and compliance tests.
   • Continuous Integration and release configuration files (e.g., CircleCI and GitHub workflows) support automated testing and deployment.

2. Analyze the File Structure:
   • Top-level Go source files (like client.go, server.go, conn.go, compression.go, mask.go, etc.) implement the core functionalities of the WebSocket protocol – managing connections, compression, masking, JSON handling, and message queues.
   • The “examples” directory consist of several subdirectories which house separate applications to demonstrate or test various aspects of the WebSocket implementation.
   • Additional testing files (e.g., *_test.go files) indicate that the project is well-tested and likely modular in its structure.
   • The presence of configuration files for CI (.circleci/config.yml and .github/release-drafter.yml) signals automated builds and releases.

3. Sketch the Main Components for the Diagram:
   • Core WebSocket Library:
     - Modules such as connection management (“conn.go”, “join.go”), masking (“mask.go”), compression (“compression.go”), and utility functions (“util.go”).
     - These represent the internal workings that adhere to the WebSocket protocol (handshake, message framing, upgrading, ping/pong handling, etc.).
   • Testing/Compliance:
     - Autobahn example (located in “examples/autobahn”) showing compliance with the Autobahn Test Suite.
     - Various test files surrounding each module.
   • Example Applications:
     - Chat, Command, Echo, and File Watch examples, each in its own directory (“examples/chat”, “examples/command”, etc.). These demonstrate how users can employ the library.
   • CI/CD Integration:
     - The CircleCI and GitHub configuration files can be noted as external processes ensuring build, test, and deployment quality.

4. Determine Relationships and Interactions:
   • The internal library components interact tightly to facilitate the WebSocket handshake, data transmission (with compression and masking), and connection management.
   • The examples utilize the library’s functions to build higher-level applications like chat or echo servers. Show these as clients or endpoints connecting to the underlying WebSocket server functionality.
   • Code dependencies are clear: the examples layer “on top” of the core library, while testing files and CI configurations validate these interactions.

5. Highlight Architectural Patterns and Principles:
   • Modular Design – around core responsibilities (connection, compression, masking, protocol compliance).
   • Separation of Concerns – the core WebSocket functionality is decoupled from the example applications, allowing usage in multiple contexts.
   • Testing and CI Integration – automated tests (in the form of *_test.go files) and continuous integration practices ensure reliability and stability.

6. Include Relevant Technologies:
   • Go (Golang) is the primary language and runtime.
   • WebSocket protocol as defined in RFC 6455.
   • CI tools from CircleCI and GitHub Actions.
   • The library may rely on Go’s net/http and other standard libraries.

7. Guidelines for Tailoring the System Diagram:
   • For this library project, start by drawing a central block representing the “Gorilla WebSocket Core Library”.
   • Around this central block, identify the key internal modules:
       - Connection Handler (shows files like conn.go, join.go).
       - Message Fragmentation & Framing (mask.go, json.go).
       - Compression Module (compression.go and related test file).
       - Utility Functions (util.go) that support overall operations.
   • From the core block, draw arrows (or lines) to the various “Example Applications” blocks (Chat, Echo, Command, Filewatch, Autobahn).
       - Emphasize how these examples “use” the core library functions.
   • Add a surrounding layer or side blocks for “Testing & CI” to show that every push triggers tests (referencing .circleci and .github configs).
   • Use directional arrows to indicate data flow, for example:
       - From client-side examples connecting to the central server.
       - From server executing connection and message handling.
   • Optionally, color-code:
       - Core modules in one color.
       - Examples in another color.
       - CI and testing as peripheral components in a lighter or distinct color.

8. Detailed Diagram Elements to Instruct:
   • Clear labels: Each block must state its role (e.g., Connection Manager, Compression Handler, Chat Example Application).
   • Directional arrows: To demonstrate client-server flows and dependency arrows between the core library and examples.
   • Use distinct shapes or colors: For example, rectangles for modules, cylinders for data stores (if any, though this project mainly focuses on protocol data flow, not persistence).
   • Optionally include notes that indicate which files reside in each component (for clarity within the team).

In summary, your diagram should present an overall architecture where the Gorilla WebSocket core (implementing critical WebSocket functionalities) is central, surrounded by various example applications that demonstrate its usage, and tethered to an automated testing/CI layer that ensures the project’s correctness and compliance with standards like the Autobahn Test Suite. This highly modular and decoupled design is key to understanding the system's robustness, and when diagramming, be as detailed as possible – each functional block and its interactions should be captured using clear labels, directional arrows, and distinct formatting (colors/shapes) to accurately represent the system’s architecture.

By following these guidelines, you will create a system diagram that not only represents the project’s technical structure but also clarifies its usage patterns and compliance mechanisms to the principal software engineer.
</explanation>
